statement: Under the specification homologated in August 2026, Beaujolais is the appellation name; Villages is a mention that may follow Beaujolais, and specified commune names may also supplement Beaujolais. CARTA therefore does not model Beaujolais-Villages as a separate current appellation.

quantity.scope: Communes in the grape-production area enumerated by the August 2026 Beaujolais specification

source_refs.locator: Chapter I, section IV.1.a: 77 Rhône communes and 11 Saône-et-Loire communes

statement: The August 2026 Beaujolais specification enumerates 88 communes in the grape-production area: 77 in Rhône and 11 in Saône-et-Loire.

quantity.scope: Communes whose grapes may qualify for the Villages mention in the August 2026 Beaujolais specification

statement: The August 2026 Beaujolais specification lists 38 communes whose grapes may qualify for the Villages mention.

scope_notes: This claim governs Beaujolais and its Villages/commune mentions, not the separate cru specifications.

source_refs.locator: Chapter I, sections II and V.1

statement: The current Beaujolais specification covers still white, rosé and red wines. White wine is made only from Chardonnay; red and rosé wine use Gamay N as the principal variety with limited accessory varieties under the specification’s percentages.

source_refs.locator: Chapter I, sections II and XII

statement: Under the current Beaujolais specification, the primeur or nouveau mention is available to red and rosé wines, not white wines.

The ten Beaujolais crus are Brouilly, Côte de Brouilly, Chénas, Chiroubles, Fleurie, Juliénas, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Régnié and Saint-Amour; each retains its own appellation identity and INAO regulatory-area representation.

scope_notes: The semi-carbonic language appears in the explanatory causal-link section, not as a universal operative vinification requirement.
statement: The current specification describes a regional vinification tradition inspired by semi-carbonic maceration, but it does not require every Beaujolais wine to undergo carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration.

source_refs.locator: Chapter X, causal link and historical description

statement: The current Beaujolais specification situates early-release trade before 1951, identifies the 13 November 1951 regulatory turn, records the third-Thursday release rule from 1985, and reports a mid-1980s peak near 500,000 hectolitres while stating that primeur never exceeded half of total Beaujolais production.
Microsatellite parentage analysis supports Gamay noir as an offspring of Pinot and Gouais blanc; Chardonnay is another offspring of the same parental pair, which does not imply stylistic equivalence.

A 1395 ordinance issued under Philip the Bold targeted Gamay in ducal Burgundy. CARTA records it as historical wine and economic regulation within its own territorial context, not as a modern Burgundy boundary statement.

resolution_needed: Do not state that the 1395 ordinance by itself documents a clean, one-step migration of Gamay from modern Burgundy into Beaujolais.
statement: The simplified claim that Gamay was banned from modern Burgundy in 1395 and consequently moved to Beaujolais in one documented migration is rejected as unsupported by the ordinance record and its historical regulatory context.

Full carbonic maceration begins with intact whole bunches in a closed, oxygen-excluding carbon-dioxide atmosphere, allowing intracellular metabolism in intact berries before pressing and completion of fermentation.

Semi-carbonic maceration is related to but distinct from full carbonic maceration: fermentation of juice released in a whole-bunch vat can generate carbon dioxide around intact berries, so ordinary yeast fermentation and some intracellular metabolism proceed together without requiring a fully established external-CO2 treatment.
Whole-cluster fermentation describes the inclusion of intact bunches and stems; by itself it does not establish whether a ferment is full carbonic, semi-carbonic or neither.

resolution_needed: Keep legal tradition, technical mechanism and producer-specific protocols separate.
statement: The generalization that all Beaujolais is carbonically fermented is rejected: the legal specification does not impose it, the techniques are distinct, and producer protocols must remain individually sourced.

Jules Chauvet was a technically engaged Beaujolais wine merchant, researcher and transmission figure; a 1963 co-authored paper documents his research on malic and lactic acid evolution during carbonic maceration, while Lapierre’s first-party history documents his later guidance to Marcel Lapierre.

resolution_needed: Describe Chauvet as a researcher and transmission figure unless independent historical evidence establishes a narrower invention claim.
statement: The claim that Jules Chauvet invented carbonic maceration is rejected: the verified 1963 record establishes research participation, not invention of the mechanism.
Jean Foillard is a Beaujolais producer based in Villié-Morgon whose documented wines include Morgon and Fleurie; CARTA keeps the producer identity separate from person:jean-foillard.

scope_notes: Importer language supports influence/following, not a proven formal bilateral mentorship.
statement: Kermit Lynch describes Jean Foillard as following Jules Chauvet’s teachings; CARTA records INFLUENCED_BY and does not promote this to formal mentorship.

scope_notes: Municipality-level orientation only; no street address or vineyard location is asserted.
statement: Jean Foillard is shown at the official municipality point for Villié-Morgon because the verified producer material establishes the municipality but not a source-fit public cellar address.
Château Thivin identifies the Geoffray family’s tenure from 1877 and presents the estate as a continuing family domaine focused principally on Côte de Brouilly and Brouilly.
Château Thivin publishes its production and visitor base at 630 route du Mont Brouilly, Odenas, with first-party GPS coordinates.

Domaine de la Grand’Cour states that Jean Dutraive acquired the estate in 1969 with nine hectares in Fleurie across Grand’Cour, Chapelle des Bois and Champagne; Jean-Louis Dutraive joined in 1977 and succeeded him in 1989.

scope_notes: Current first-party estate protocol; it is not a legal rule for Fleurie, Brouilly or Beaujolais generally.
statement: Domaine de la Grand’Cour describes hand-harvested whole bunches placed uncrushed and undestemmed into low-temperature tanks saturated with carbon dioxide, followed by spontaneous fermentation to pressing without added sulfite or oenological products except intervention if a problem occurs.
Domaine de la Grand’Cour publishes its production base at 156 route de la Grand’Cour, Fleurie; CARTA geocodes that address as a point and does not use it as vineyard geometry.

resolution_needed: Do not publish a total-hectare measure until the current source’s 57-hectare headline and 37 + 18 hectare subtotal are reconciled.
statement: Domaine des Terres Dorées is based in Charnay and maintains vineyard activity in the southern Beaujolais area and in several crus; CARTA retains the current source’s acreage arithmetic as unresolved rather than manufacturing a corrected total.

scope_notes: The sources describe entrusted operation and development, not a proven asset sale or Jean-Paul Brun’s retirement.
statement: From the 2024 harvest, Jean-Paul Brun entrusted operation and development of Domaine des Terres Dorées to Domaines Roger Zannier, while the announcement says Brun would remain involved in a five-year transition focused on making the wines.
Domaine des Terres Dorées is shown at its current public address, 565 route d’Alix, Charnay; the point represents the production/business base, not vineyard holdings.
Domaine Marcel Lapierre is shown at its first-party address, 588 rue Rabelais, Villié-Morgon; the point represents the domaine base, not its Morgon or Beaujolais vineyard parcels.

Mont Brouilly is a physical hill: Côte de Brouilly occupies slopes on the hill, while Brouilly is a separate surrounding cru area. Neither appellation boundary is a vineyard-parcel map, and the hill is not itself an appellation.
Py hill is a physical feature above Villié-Morgon associated with Morgon; CARTA keeps the hill distinct from the Morgon appellation and from the named Côte du Py wine-site identity.

resolution_needed: Add bilateral mentorship only from direct evidence; retain group membership and narrower influence relationships separately.
statement: The blanket assertion that Jules Chauvet formally mentored every member of the Gang of Four is rejected; direct guidance is documented for Marcel Lapierre, while Foillard is recorded only with the narrower INFLUENCED_BY relationship supported by importer language.

Beaujolais is one appellation with governed Villages and commune-name mentions alongside ten separate cru appellations; shared Gamay importance does not collapse their legal areas, physical places or producer practices.
